notes: Slice 'essay': source material for the opening prose 'What Privacy Is: A Short History of an Idea'. Contents: 45 facts (one-sentence statements, each with 1-4 sources carrying verbatim quotes), 16 pull quotes, a 7-paragraph outline (every fact is placed once), 2 quantities and 5 myths. No mapped events - chronology lives in the other slices; facts here overlap with some of them (Warren and Brandeis, BVerfG 1983, UDHR/ICCPR, IEEE 7012, the cypherpunks) by design so the essay can stand alone. METHOD: every CONFIRMED quote was fetched with tools/fetch-text.py and passed --check (all 2026-09-23). Where the canonical host blocks scripts (bepress/Digital Commons repositories, Legifrance, OHCHR, Wiley), the quote was read from an Internet Archive copy (URL given as read) or from another official copy (French Interior Ministry PDF for Code civil art. 9; University of Minnesota Human Rights Library for General Comment 16; Crossref API for the Altman 1977 abstract; Quran.com API for Qur'an translations). Several classic statements are quoted through reliable secondary scholarship because the books are in copyright and not openly online: Westin 1967 (via Solove 2002 and Frontiers in Veterinary Science 2022), Thomson 1975, Gavison 1980, Moore 1984 and Miller 1971 (via Solove 2002), Arendt 1958 (via Komamura 2019, Washington University Law Review), Altman 1977 (publisher abstract plus Acquisti et al. 2020). Each such source note says so. COULD NOT VERIFY / GAPS: OED first-use dates (subscription) - Etymonline and Merriam-Webster disagree on the earliest 'privacy' form (Etymonline: privatie late 14c., privacy 1590s; M-W: 15th century), stated as such; Lewis & Short (Perseus) entry text for privo is not extractable by the helper; the attribution of 'la vie privée doit être murée' to Royer-Collard (1819) or Talleyrand is unverified - Littré gives it unattributed; Rybczynski's Home and Ariès/Duby's History of Private Life were not read directly (architecture facts rest on Solove 2002, which cites them); the Mishnah fact's 'measure of privacy' is a modern translator's gloss; the Constitute count (171/188) is our own computation from its API and reflects text-based coding; Fred Cate's critique of notice-and-choice was not added; Doc Searls's own weblog returns 403 to scripts, so his 2019 Linux Journal column and the ProjectVRM post are used instead. Contested points are flagged contested:true (Chinese yinsi and traditional Chinese privacy; Littré maxim attribution). HOUSEKEEPING: the session scratchpad is shared between researchers; during this run I inadvertently executed another researcher's scratchpad build.py (which had overwritten mine), which rewrote research/verify/dataprotection-2.json from that researcher's own script - the content should be identical to what their script produces, but the owner may wish to re-run it.

facts.statement: The English word 'private' comes from Latin privatus, 'set apart (from what is public), belonging to oneself (not to the state)', the past participle of privare, 'to bereave, deprive, rob, strip' - so the root carries both 'one's own' and 'deprived of'.

sources.quote: from Latin privatus "set apart (from what is public), belonging to oneself (not to the state), peculiar, personal," used in contrast to publicus , communis.
sources.note: Etymonline is a compiled dictionary that draws on the OED, Barnhart and Klein; spacing before commas is as rendered on the page. Lewis & Short (Perseus) gives privo as "To bereave, deprive, rob, strip" but its entry text is not extractable by the repo helper.

facts.statement: The Online Etymology Dictionary dates the noun 'privacy' to the 1590s, first meaning 'a private or personal matter, a secret' and from c. 1600 'seclusion', with an earlier form 'privatie' in the late 14th century; it dates the sense 'freedom from intrusion or interference' to 1814. Dictionaries disagree on the first date: Merriam-Webster puts the first known use of the 'seclusion' sense in the 15th century.

sources.institution: Online Etymology Dictionary (Douglas Harper)
sources.title: privacy (n.)
sources.quote: 1590s, "a private or personal matter, a secret;" c. 1600 as "seclusion, state of being in retirement from company or the knowledge and observation of others," from private (adj.) + abstract noun suffix -cy . Meaning "state of freedom from intrusion or interference" is from 1814. Earlier was privatie (late 14c. as "secret, mystery;" c. 1400 as "a secret, secret deed; solitude, privacy"), from Old French privauté .
sources.note: Dictionaries differ on the first date: Merriam-Webster gives the 15th century for its sense 1a, reflecting the Middle English privatie/privetee forms. Treat "late 14th-15th century (as privatie), 1590s (as privacy)" as the safe statement.

facts.statement: Hannah Arendt argued in The Human Condition (1958) that for the ancient Greeks privacy was 'privative' - a life lived only in private was deprived of the public realm and 'not fully human' - whereas modern privacy's 'most relevant function' is 'to shelter the intimate'.

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: In ancient feeling the privative trait of privacy, indicated in the word itself, was all-important; it meant literally a state of being deprived of something, and even of the highest and most human of man's capacities. A man who lived only a private life, who like the slave was not permitted to enter the public realm, or like the barbarian had chosen not to establish such a realm, was not fully human.
sources.note: Komamura quotes Arendt verbatim (Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, University of Chicago Press, 1958; p. 38 of the 2nd ed., 1998). The book itself is in copyright and was not read from a publisher copy.

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: The decisive historical fact is that modern privacy in its most relevant function, to shelter the intimate, was discovered as the opposite not of the political sphere but of the social, to which it is therefore more closely and authentically related.
sources.note: Komamura (pp. 1344-45) quotes Arendt, The Human Condition (1958), p. 38, verbatim. His own abstract adds: "privacy has been a relational concept since the beginnings of western political thought."

issues: The statement quotes 'not fully human', but neither source quote contained that phrase. Komamura's block quote of Arendt continues into it, so quote 0 has been extended to cover it.
The note on quote 1 gives 'pp. 1344-45'. The passage (Arendt's 'We no longer think primarily of deprivation ...' paragraph) falls entirely after the page-1345 running head, so it is on p. 1345.

facts.statement: Philosophical accounts of privacy usually start with the Greeks. Aristotle's split between the household (oikos) and the political community (polis) is the standard starting point for philosophical discussions of privacy, and his Politics contrasts what is one's own (idion) with what is common (koinon).

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: In the ancient Greek thought, political community (polis) is not just different from but stands in direct opposition to the natural community whose center is the home and the family (oikos).
sources.note: Komamura, p. 1341, paraphrasing Arendt, The Human Condition (1998 ed.), p. 28: "the distinction between a private and a public sphere of life corresponds to the household and the political realms".

sources.institution: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Beate Roessler and Judith DeCew)
sources.title: Privacy (substantive revision 19 October 2023)
sources.quote: Aristotle's distinction between the public sphere of politics and political activity, the polis , and the private or domestic sphere of the family, the oikos , is the starting point for philosophical discussions of privacy ( Politics 1253b, 1259b).
sources.note: Spacing around "polis ," and "( Politics" is as extracted from the HTML (italic tags).

sources.institution: MIT Internet Classics Archive (Benjamin Jowett translation)
sources.title: Aristotle, Politics, Book Two, Part III
sources.quote: For that which is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it. Every one thinks chiefly of his own, hardly at all of the common interest; and only when he is himself concerned as an individual.
sources.note: Politics 2.1261b33-35. Greek (Perseus, Perseus:text:1999.01.0057): "ἥκιστα γὰρ ἐπιμελείας τυγχάνει τὸ πλείστων κοινόν: τῶν γὰρ ἰδίων μάλιστα φροντίζουσιν, τῶν δὲ κοινῶν ἧττον" - koinon (common) against idion (one's own). The Greek was read on Perseus but the repo helper cannot extract it, so the English is quoted.

facts.note: For the Greek idion/koinon vocabulary see the Aristotle fact. Aristotle here argues about property and care, not "privacy" in the modern sense; use it for the vocabulary of own vs common, not as an ancient privacy right.

issues: 'Greek thought drew the first map' is an overstated priority claim. No source says the Greeks were first to separate private from public. The SEP only calls Aristotle's polis/oikos distinction 'the starting point for philosophical discussions of privacy'. The wording has been softened.

The note on source 0 says Komamura's sentence paraphrases Arendt p. 28. In fact that sentence carries footnote 9, 'ARENDT, supra note 8, at 24'. The quoted line 'the distinction between a private and a public sphere of life corresponds to the household and the political realms' is the next sentence, footnote 10, 'Id. at 28'.

facts.statement: The Chinese word for privacy, yinsi (隐私), joins yin (隐), 'hide', and si (私), 'private'. In a 2005 law-review article, Cao Jingchun distinguished it from a near-homophone 'most often used in legislation', translated as 'privacy', 'personal secret' or 'shameful secret', which 'usually means something negative'. Because the two words were 'used confusingly', he wrote, 'it was initially common for Chinese to misunderstand privacy as relating to shameful secrets'.

sources.institution: Victoria University of Wellington Law Review (vol. 36, no. 3)
sources.title: Cao Jingchun, 'Protecting the Right to Privacy in China'
sources.quote: Yin and si are two words in Chinese: yin means "hide" and si means "private".
sources.note: The PDF text has lost the Chinese characters; Cao distinguishes two near-homophones (commonly written 阴私, a shameful secret, and 隐私, privacy). Characters in the statement are supplied from the NPC source below, not from Cao.

sources.institution: Victoria University of Wellington Law Review (vol. 36, no. 3)
sources.title: Cao Jingchun, 'Protecting the Right to Privacy in China'
sources.quote: It was initially common for Chinese to misunderstand privacy as relating to shameful secrets.

sources.institution: Victoria University of Wellington Law Review (vol. 36, no. 3)
sources.title: Cao Jingchun, 'Protecting the Right to Privacy in China'
sources.quote: It is this word which is most often used in legislation and is most familiar to Chinese lawyers. It is translated into English as "privacy", "personal secret" or "shameful secret". However it usually means something negative. In contrast, the related word "Yinsi" is closer to Western ideas of privacy.
sources.note: --check FOUND. This is the passage that actually carries the three translations. Cao applies them to the legislative, negative word, which he contrasts with 'Yinsi' (隐私), the word 'closer to Western ideas of privacy'.

sources.institution: Wiktionary
sources.title: 隱 (Chinese)
sources.quote: to hide ; to cover ; to shield
sources.note: --check FOUND (the spacing is as extracted). 隱 is the traditional form of 隐, the yin of 隐私. The 隱私 entry (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E9%9A%B1%E7%A7%81) gives 'private business ; secrets ; personal matters ; privacy' (FOUND). The 陰私 entry gives 'hidden secret' (FOUND). Wiktionary is a collaborative dictionary, so this is secondary support only.

facts.note: Contested: whether traditional China lacked a privacy concept is debated; Cao himself argues privacy "was protected, to some extent, in ancient China" though neither the word nor the modern concept existed.

issues: The statement conflates two words. In Cao, the translations 'privacy', 'personal secret' or 'shameful secret' belong to a word 'most often used in legislation' that 'usually means something negative'. Cao sets it 'in contrast' to 'the related word "Yinsi"', which 'is closer to Western ideas of privacy' and which he defines from the Modern Chinese Dictionary as 'a personal thing people do not wish to tell others or disclose in public'. That definition matches 隐私. The negative word is the near-homophone generally written 阴私 (Wiktionary: 'hidden secret'). The PDF has lost the Chinese characters, so this identification rests on the dictionary definitions (Cao cites pp. 1363 and 1368, i.e. two separate entries). The statement wrongly gave all three translations to 隐私.
'Legal scholar' overstates Cao's standing. The article's author note says it was 'Submitted as part of the LLM programme at Victoria University of Wellington.'
Cao's gloss 'yin means "hide"' is attached in his text to the negative, legislative word. For 隐 = 'hide' an independent dictionary source has been added.

facts.statement: China's Civil Code (2020), Article 1032, gives the word a legal definition: privacy (隐私) is a natural person's tranquillity of private life and the private space, private activities and private information that they do not wish others to know.

facts.statement: Japanese uses the loanword puraibashii (プライバシー), a phonetic rendering of the English 'privacy'. Masao Horibe, then chairman of Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission, said in 2017 that the term came into wide use owing partly to the Tokyo District Court's ruling of 28 September 1964 in a suit over Yukio Mishima's novel After the Banquet, which recognised privacy as a legally protected right for the first time.

sources.institution: Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan (speech by Chairman Masao Horibe, ICDPPC, Hong Kong)
sources.title: Privacy Culture and Data Protection Laws in Japan
sources.quote: In the ruling on the case in 1964, the Tokyo District Court recognized privacy as a right to be protected under the Japanese law for the first time in history.

sources.institution: Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan (speech by Chairman Masao Horibe, ICDPPC, Hong Kong)
sources.title: Privacy Culture and Data Protection Laws in Japan
sources.quote: Due to this court decision and many other backgrounds, the Japanese term of "puraibashii", which is a phonetic spelling of an English word "privacy", has been widely used in our society.

sources.institution: Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training (JILPT Report No. 14)
sources.title: Ryoko Sakuraba, 'Protection of Personal Information and Privacy in the Japanese Workplace'
sources.quote: Tokyo District Court (28 September 1964), 15-9 Kaminshu 2317.
sources.note: Gives the exact date of the "Utage no Ato" (After the Banquet) judgment. The katakana プライバシー is standard Japanese orthography and is not quoted from these sources.

issues: 'Japan's data-protection chairman Masao Horibe has said' reads as present tense. The source is a September 2017 speech, so he should be described as 'then chairman' of the Personal Information Protection Commission.

'It spread after' the ruling slightly overstates Horibe. He says the term became widely used 'Due to this court decision and many other backgrounds'. The loanword also predates the ruling: the JILPT report cites Masami Ito, 'Puraibashi no Kenri' (Iwanami 1963).

facts.statement: German has two words for two ideas: the everyday Privatsphäre, a protected 'narrower realm of personal life', and informationelle Selbstbestimmung, the right to 'informational self-determination' that the Federal Constitutional Court recognised on 15 December 1983 - the individual's authority, in principle, to decide on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act)
sources.quote: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany), official English translation
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act)

sources.quote: La vie privée doit être murée, il n'est pas permis de chercher et de faire connaître ce qui se passe dans la maison d'un particulier.
sources.note: Littré gives the maxim without attribution. It is widely attributed to Pierre-Paul Royer-Collard (c. 1819) and sometimes to Talleyrand (Stendhal, 1823); the attribution was not verified from a primary source.

sources.quote: Je n'ose continuer de peur d'entreprendre sur la vie privée d'un citoyen, qui, comme l'a si bien dit M. de Talleyrand, doit être murée
sources.note: --check FOUND. This is Stendhal's letter of 31 Oct. 1823, as quoted by Éd. Fournier (Feuilleton de la Patrie, 14 juill. 1868) in Littré's Remarque. Fournier opens: 'J'ai cru d'abord, comme bien des gens. que c'était Royer-Collard [qui avait créé cette expression]' (also FOUND). This shows the Royer-Collard attribution was already doubted in the 19th century.

facts.note: Attribution contested. Littré prints the maxim unattributed under 'privé', but the entry's Remarque quotes Édouard Fournier (La Patrie, 14 July 1868). Fournier had thought it Royer-Collard's, then found Stendhal (letter of 31 Oct. 1823) crediting Talleyrand. Quote it as Littré's, not as Royer-Collard's or Talleyrand's.

issues: The note on the Littré source says 'Littré gives the maxim without attribution'. That holds only for the definition line. The same Littré entry has a REMARQUE quoting Édouard Fournier (Feuilleton de la Patrie, 14 July 1868). Fournier had believed Royer-Collard coined 'le mur de la vie privée', then found a Stendhal letter of 31 Oct. 1823 crediting Talleyrand. The attribution debate is therefore in Littré itself, and the notes have been corrected with a source added. The statement itself is accurate.

facts.statement: In Arabic-Islamic usage the idea closest to privacy is often hurma - what is sacred or unlawful to look at without permission, including the home - alongside awrah, what must be covered; the Qur'an tells believers not to enter others' houses until welcomed (24:27) and forbids spying (49:12).

facts.statement: Alan Westin's Privacy and Freedom (1967), written for a New York City Bar committee on science and law, defined privacy as 'the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others', and argued that it preserves autonomy, release from role-playing, self-evaluation and protected communication.

Read from the Internet Archive copy of the GW Law repository PDF (the live repository returns 403 to scripts). Canonical: https://scholarship.law.gwu.edu/faculty_publications/933/

issues: No error found. The definition is Westin's (Privacy and Freedom, 1967, p. 7, per Solove n. 111, 'Westin, supra note 4, at 7'). The Bar committee and Carnegie funding come from a 1968 review written soon after the book appeared.

Minor, no change needed: 'release from role-playing' is the 1968 book note's paraphrase. Westin's own name for this function is 'emotional release', and his four functions are personal autonomy, emotional release, self-evaluation, and limited and protected communication. The paraphrase is fair.

facts.statement: Westin argued, drawing on studies of animal behaviour and territoriality, that the human need for privacy 'may well be rooted' in our animal origins, and that people and animals share several basic mechanisms for claiming privacy.

facts.statement: The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code (compiled c. 200 CE), bars a person from opening new windows into a courtyard he shares with partners, and from opening a doorway opposite a neighbour's doorway or a window opposite a neighbour's window onto such a courtyard - a rule a modern English translation glosses as ensuring residents 'a measure of privacy'.

sources.note: This clause is the translator's explanatory interpolation (unbolded in the Davidson edition), not the Mishnah's own words. The phrase "damage by seeing" (hezek re'iyah) is from the Talmud (Bava Batra 2b-3a) and is not quoted from this page.

facts.note: The "c. 200 CE" compilation date and the term hezek re'iyah are standard but not stated on the cited page; treat them as context.

issues: The statement merges two separate rules in Bava Batra 3:7 and pins the privacy gloss on the wrong one. The Mishnah (a) bars a partner from opening new windows into a jointly owned courtyard, and (b) bars opening 'an entrance opposite another entrance or a window opposite another window toward a courtyard belonging to partners'. The translator's gloss 'so as to ensure that the residents will enjoy a measure of privacy' is attached to (b), not to a general ban on windows or doorways 'facing' the courtyard.

The quotes are verbatim, and the source note correctly marks the privacy clause as the Koren/Steinsaltz translator's unbolded interpolation. The dating context (c. 200 CE) is consistent with the standard account that Judah ha-Nasi compiled the Mishnah in the late 2nd or early 3rd century. The note's claim about hezek re'iyah in Bava Batra 2b is also correct: the Sefaria Davidson English for Bava Batra 2b discusses 'whether damage caused by sight is called damage'.

facts.statement: Of the 188 national constitutions in force in the Comparative Constitutions Project's Constitute database, 171 (about nine in ten) are coded as providing a right to privacy. Among the 17 exceptions are India and France, whose constitutional texts are silent on privacy and where courts and statute protect it instead; others, such as Japan and Canada, do guard homes, papers or searches in their texts but are not coded under this topic, so the count reflects Constitute's coding.

sources.title: Topics: Right to privacy
sources.quote: Grants individuals protection against government intrusion into their property, papers, person, or communications without proper authorization. Also protects against such intrusions by private individuals.
sources.note: Topic definition. Counts computed on 2026-09-23 from the Constitute API: 171 in-force constitutions returned by https://www.constituteproject.org/service/constopicsearch?key=privacy&in_force=true&lang=en out of 188 in force (https://www.constituteproject.org/service/constitutions?in_force=true&lang=en). In-force constitutions not coded for privacy: Afghanistan, Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, Austria, Bahamas, Brunei, Canada, Czech Republic, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Palau, Samoa, Singapore, Sri Lanka. Coding is of constitutional text only.

sources.note: --check FOUND. The same page has Art. 21: 'No censorship shall be maintained, nor shall the secrecy of any means of communication be violated.' (--check FOUND). Japan_1946 is nevertheless absent from the privacy topic list, which shows that the 17 exceptions include coding gaps as well as constitutions that are silent on privacy. The date is promulgation (3 Nov 1946); the Constitution took effect on 3 May 1947.

facts.note: The count is our computation from the Constitute API (re-run 2026-09-23: 171 of 188), not a figure the project publishes; it depends on Constitute's coding and on which constitutional documents it holds (e.g. Czechia's separate Charter of Fundamental Rights and Austria's constitutional-rank ECHR are not in the texts coded). Japan (Art. 35 searches, Art. 21 secrecy of communication) and Canada (Charter s. 8) have search-and-seizure text that Constitute does not code as privacy, while the similar US Fourth Amendment is coded, so 171 is a conservative count. The claim that courts protect privacy in India and France rests on the Puttaswamy and Article 9 facts elsewhere in this file.

issues: The count reproduces. On 2026-09-23 the Constitute API returned 171 constitutions for key=privacy&in_force=true and 188 in-force constitutions (188 distinct countries). All 171 are among the 188, and the 17 uncoded ones match the note's list exactly. 171/188 = 91%, so 'about nine in ten' is right.

Wrong example: Japan is not a country where 'courts rather than the text' protect privacy. Japan's 1946 Constitution, as printed on Constitute itself, says in Art. 35 'The right of all persons to be secure in their homes, papers and effects against entries, searches and seizures shall not be impaired except upon warrant' and in Art. 21 'nor shall the secrecy of any means of communication be violated'. Both fall squarely within Constitute's own topic definition ('protection against government intrusion into their property, papers, person, or communications'), and the near-identical US Fourth Amendment is coded for privacy (United_States_of_America_1992 is among the 171). Japan's absence is a coding gap, not missing text. Canada is the same case: Charter s. 8, 'Everyone has the right to be secure against unreasonable search or seizure', is in Canada_2011 but not coded.

India and France are good examples. A search of Constitute's English texts of India_2023 and France_2024 finds no 'privacy' or 'private life'. For France, the right comes from statute (Civil Code art. 9) and from Conseil constitutionnel rulings, not from the courts alone, so the wording should say 'courts and statute'.
The record note says the Japan claim 'rests on the ... 1964 facts'. That 1964 Tokyo District Court tort ruling does not show the constitutional text is silent, so the note needs the same correction.

France's press law of 11 May 1868 already punished publishing information 'relative à un fait de la vie privée', and Warren and Brandeis cited it. The 1791 French Constitution protected 'actions of private life' against calumny. What 1890 marks is the named common-law 'right to privacy'. The Griswold dissent says the phrase 'appears first to have gained currency' from the Warren and Brandeis article.

myths.claim: Chinese and Japanese have no word for privacy.
myths.correction: Chinese has yinsi (隐私), which Article 1032 of China's 2020 Civil Code defines as a person's tranquillity of private life and the private space, activities and information they do not wish others to know; its reception was clouded by a near-homophone long used in legislation to mean shameful secrets, and legal writer Cao Jingchun noted in 2005 that Chinese people initially often misunderstood privacy that way. Japanese uses the loanword puraibashii, introduced by scholars in the early 1960s and, according to data-protection chairman Masao Horibe, widely used owing to a 1964 Tokyo District Court judgment 'and many other backgrounds'. The words are newer or differently weighted than the English one - not absent.

issues: The correction repeats the conflation already fixed in fact chinese-yinsi-shameful-secret (verify/essay-1). It says yinsi (隐私) was 'long carrying a connotation of shameful secrets'. The only source for the shameful-secret sense is Cao Jingchun (VUWLR 2005), and he attaches that sense to a near-homophone 'most often used in legislation' ('translated into English as "privacy", "personal secret" or "shameful secret". However it usually means something negative'). He contrasts it with 'the related word "Yinsi"', which 'is closer to Western ideas of privacy'. He says the confusion between the two words led Chinese people at first to misunderstand privacy as shameful secrets.

'Japanese adopted the loanword puraibashii, which spread after a 1964 Tokyo court judgment' overstates the source. Horibe (PPC chairman, 2017) says the term became widely used 'Due to this court decision and many other backgrounds'. The loanword was in print before the ruling: the JILPT report says the concept 'was adopted after the introduction of this theory by academics in the 1960s' and cites Masami Ito, Puraibashi no Kenri (Iwanami 1963). The ruling was 28 September 1964.

Checked OK: the NPC page quotes Civil Code Art. 1032 verbatim ('民法典第1032条规定：“隐私是...”'). The Civil Code was adopted on 28 May 2020 and took effect on 1 January 2021, so '2020 Civil Code' is right. The verdict MISLEADING is defensible: both words exist today, and the kernel of truth is that one is a loanword and the other has a shifted connotation.
